headline: Associate Director @ EY | Doctoral Candidate @ Purdue University | AI and Cyber
about:
I am a technology enthusiast and optimist looking to make technology and data more secure and resilient.

I currently serve as an Associate Director in EY’s Technology Risk Management practice. My role focuses on helping EY member firms adhere to internal and external security, data, and regulatory requirements. I assist member firms in enhancing effective and efficient technology governance and oversight through technical reviews, consultations, and assessments. Additionally, I assist Global AI governance, risk, and control initiatives to ensure AI products and services align with the firm’s strategic technology risk management processes. I am in the final year of my Doctoral studies at Purdue University, specializing in AI and information security. 

My previous experience includes various cybersecurity roles at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago and teaching undergraduate courses at Purdue University Northwest as an adjunct lecturer. 

I am dedicated to continuous learning in cybersecurity and IT, enhancing my skills through academic degrees, certifications, and speaking engagements worldwide. My research interests encompass AI security and risk management, cybersecurity compliance, identity and access management, data protection, and more. 

Feel free to contact me for research collaborations, speaking engagements, and other opportunities.

about:
Dynamic, strategic leader with over 18 years of global experience in financial services, specializing in enterprise data management, technology strategy, and digital transformation. Proven track record in designing and executing holistic data programs, including strategy, architecture, analytics, master data management (MDM), lineage, integration, and metadata.

Leveraging my deep data management expertise and recognition that data serves as the core currency of modern technology ecosystems, I empower clients to enhance operational efficiency, optimize processes, and achieve tangible business results. As a trusted advisor, I steer IT modernization efforts via cloud migrations, AI-powered automation, agentic process orchestration, and cutting-edge innovations.

I unlock growth and amplify outcomes by integrating data and AI to synchronize emerging technologies with business goals, accelerating transformative initiatives.

Adept at forging robust client partnerships and fostering cross-functional teamwork, I excel in guiding intricate global projects from conception to delivery. My proficiency spans IT operations, agile and SDLC frameworks, orchestration tools, automation platforms, and large-scale enterprise transformations.

Blending sharp analytical acumen with exceptional leadership and communication abilities, I consistently deliver innovative, scalable solutions that advance strategic objectives.

experience.position: Senior Manager | FSO Advisory - Process Orchestration, Automation & AI
experience.description:
Providing Automation, Cloud, Digital, and Transformation services across Asset Management, Insurance, Banking, and Capital Markets. Focused on rationalizing incumbent technologies by partnering with industry-leading vendors to define target state and interim state architecture blueprints that are agile and responsive to evolving external influences. This includes developing associated roadmaps, strategies, architecture principles, and patterns rooted in event-driven design and the API economy.

Leveraging the power of data, AI, and agentic orchestration to reimagine enterprise operations—enabling intelligent, autonomous workflows that adapt dynamically to business needs. Leading vendor selection for target platforms, and defining robust content and data migration strategies, including seamless transitions from on-premise to cloud-native environments.

Driving end-to-end process improvement by modernizing legacy operations, reducing costs, enhancing operational efficiency, mitigating risk, and minimizing maintenance overhead. Delivering workforce optimization through intelligent workload routing, maximizing straight-through processing, and ultimately improving customer experience and business outcomes.

Utilize a data-driven approach to identify opportunities for Robotics Process Automation (RPA), Cognitive Automation, and agentic workflows—targeting cost reduction, enhanced straight-through processing (STP), improved operational risk controls, and scalable, future-ready solutions that enable digital transformation.

Draw on a strong foundation in data architecture, integration, and governance to ensure automation efforts are underpinned by clean, reliable, and well-structured data—maximizing automation accuracy, consistency, and long-term value.

Practice development initiatives include authoring thought leadership pieces and Points of View (PoVs) on RPA and Cognitive Automation, designing accelerators, reusable templates, and implementation frameworks, and contributing to talent acquisition strategies to scale the practice effectively.

Lead business development initiatives through the creation of proposals, client discussion materials, and Statements of Work (SOW), helping position automation and data as dual enablers of transformation.

Successfully stand up enterprise-grade RPA programs—leading end-to-end activities such as proof of concepts, roadmap definition, operating model design (including Center of Excellence setup), and the full RPA program lifecycle: process identification, prioritization, architecture, design, configuration, testing, and production deployment.

experience.position: Senior Manager  |  FSO Advisory - Data & Analyitcs
experience.description:

Practice development initiatives include authoring Points of View on key topics such as Self-Service Analytics, Data Lake vs. Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW), Customer 360°, and Securities 360°, as well as developing frameworks and accelerators to support scalable data management programs and talent acquisition strategies.

Lead business development efforts for the practice, including the creation of client proposals (RFI/RFP responses), discussion materials, and Statements of Work (SOW), helping organizations unlock the full potential of their data assets.

Provide comprehensive data management advisory services to financial services organizations, leveraging core capabilities in data strategy, data integration, Master Data Management (MDM), and Big Data to drive enterprise-wide transformation. Advise clients on designing and implementing scalable data architectures and integration frameworks that support regulatory compliance, operational efficiency, and strategic insights.

Project engagements have included Enterprise Risk Data Integration, large-scale MDM implementations, and Enterprise Service Bus (ESB) integration—ensuring seamless data flow across critical systems and establishing a single source of truth for key data domains.

Support clients in developing end-to-end data strategies that align with business goals, from current state assessments and gap analyses to future state roadmaps encompassing data governance, metadata management, and data quality.

Contribute to internal practice development through the creation of accelerators, frameworks, and reusable assets, and lead business development initiatives including proposal development, client workshops, and strategic solutioning for data transformation programs.

Implemented and managed global enterprise reference data and financial accounting solutions at major banks/custodians. 

Projects included system revitalizations (centralized enterprise platform for customer & counter party data), Strategic In house Initiatives to consolidate all Customers, Securities & Pricing Data onto the GoldenSource Enterprise Data Management Platform (EDM) making GoldenSource the Data Hub for the entire financial organization for Securities, Pricing, Customer & Counterparty Data.

headline: Investment Banking & Venture Capital | Managing Partner @ Mavka Capital | M&A, Capital Raising & Corporate Finance | Mobility, Energy Transition, Embodied AI and Robotics | Best-Selling Author | Speaker
about:
Vitaly M. Golomb is an entrepreneur, investor, investment banker and Managing Partner of the Mavka ecosystem—an integrated platform serving innovative companies from startup to scale across frontier tech sectors.

The Mavka platform includes:
- Mavka Capital - Corporate finance advisory and investment banking
- Mavka Growth - Go-to-market acceleration for Series A to Series B companies
- Mavka Ventures - Seed stage embodied AI fund 

With 20+ years as a Silicon Valley entrepreneur, investment banker, and venture capitalist, Vitaly brings a unique perspective having been on all sides of the table—as a founder seeking capital, as an investor deploying it, and as a banker structuring complex transactions.

As a Founding Partner of HP's corporate venture arm and former Partner at Drake Star, he has led dozens of M&A and capital markets transactions across North America, Europe, and Asia. His experience spans Series A through IPO-stage companies, with deep expertise in mobility tech, energy infrastructure, and AI-driven industrial applications.

Vitaly is the best-selling author of "Accelerated Startup" (ranked among top startup books of all time) and prolific writer on innovation, as well as behavioral and political economics. He holds active Series 7, 79, 63, and 24 securities licenses and is a Registered Representative of Finalis Securities LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC.

Whether you're a founder needing growth acceleration, seeking capital, or exploring strategic alternatives, the Mavka ecosystem provides comprehensive support from a network of leaders who have successfully built, funded, and advised innovative companies for decades.

featured.title: The Weight of Tinsel: A Letter to Those Who Carry December
featured.subtitle: Vitaly Golomb on LinkedIn

slides.title: The Weight of Tinsel: A Letter to Those Who Carry December
slides.subtitle: Vitaly Golomb on LinkedIn
slides.description: The world dons its festive mask again. Lights strung like promises along every street. Carols piped through speaker systems in lobbies where I’ve pitched, where I’ve won, where I’ve lost. The calendar flips toward year’s end, and while others count down to celebration, we — those of us who’ve built companies from nothing — count something else entirely. We count the runway. We count the pipeline. We count the days until the world gets back to work. We count the hours until December finally lets go. The Pavlovian Shudder There’s a strange alchemy that occurs in an entrepreneur’s nervous system after Thanksgiving. While others feel the warmth of approaching festivities, we sense the cold calculations of December. It’s Pavlovian, conditioned by years of watching the business world slow to a crawl when we need it most. The inbox that once flooded us becomes a trickle. The “let’s circle back in January” becomes the refrain of our sleepless nights. For service companies, December is a beautiful yet brutal wasteland. Clients go dark. Procurement comes to a halt. The billable hours that sustain teams and families disappear into holiday parties we’re too anxious to fully enjoy. We smile at our gatherings while mental spreadsheets run behind our eyes, recalculating margins and survival. For startups in the midst of capital raises, the holidays are a special kind of purgatory. That term sheet that was “almost ready” before Thanksgiving? It’s now trapped in the amber of year-end, suspended between “yes” and “we’ll finalize in Q1.” VCs go on ski trips. Angel investors focus on family. And the entrepreneur — the one who’s been running on fumes and belief — must somehow keep the momentum going in a vacuum, keep the team motivated when the bank account speaks louder than any pep talk, and when the silence from investors feels like rejection disguised as holiday cheer. The Arithmetic of Anxiety I know this weight. Not as an observer, not as someone who read about it in a case study, but as someone who has carried it through more than twenty Decembers. For over 85% of my twenty-five-plus-year career, I’ve been the one responsible. The CEO. The founder. The person whose signature was on the lease, the payroll, the promises made to people who believed in a vision that sometimes felt as fragile as the ornaments hanging in the office we couldn’t quite afford but needed to project success. I’ve sat in December darkness — the literal kind, when everyone else has gone home to their families — and done the math. The harsh, relentless math of cash flow, hiring decisions, and the question that haunts every leader: Who stays? Who goes? And how do I make this choice when these aren’t just employees but people with mortgages and children and dreams of their own? I’ve watched the faces of talented people as they received news that should never come in December. I’ve seen the moment when understanding dawns — that their year-end bonus won’t materialize, that the raise they planned around won’t happen, that the security they thought they had has vanished in a boardroom conversation. I’ve been the architect of that moment, and I’ve carried every instance of it. The Violence of December Layoffs There is a particular brutality to layoffs at the end of the year. To become the person who sends someone — a breadwinner, a parent, a human being with obligations and bills and people depending on them — into the uncertainty of January with a severance package and well-wishes. To watch the holiday lights mock the darkness you’ve just brought to someone’s doorstep. The world doesn’t pause for their anxiety. Holiday shopping bills arrive regardless of circumstances. Children still believe in magic, while their parents lie awake calculating how long unemployment will last. The rent doesn’t care that it’s the season of giving. The mortgage holder doesn’t acknowledge the spirit of charity. Life’s obligations march forward indifferently, and we — those of us who had to make the decision — we carry that weight alongside everything else. There is a particular ache to it. You’re trying to save the company, trying to preserve something for everyone who remains, and in that effort, you’ve become the harbinger of someone else’s crisis. You’ve become the memory they will associate with December for years to come. Not the joy, but the layoff. The Performance of Leadership There’s a peculiar isolation that comes with entrepreneurial leadership during the holidays. At parties, people ask how business is going, and you’ve learned the script: “Good! Busy!” Because the truth doesn’t fit comfortably between the eggnog and the small talk. The truth is terrifying. The truth is that you’re three months from running out of cash, that you laid off 30% of your team last week and you’re not sure the company will survive Q1, that you haven’t slept properly since October. Your family sees you there but not fully present. They see you in body, but your mind is elsewhere. While they’re discussing vacation plans, you’re running different scenarios. While they’re debating which movie to watch, you’re composing an email to investors explaining why the numbers didn’t hit where you said they would. While they’re raising a glass to the new year, you’re calculating whether you can make payroll. The entrepreneur’s December is a performance. We perform confidence for our teams. We perform optimism for our investors. We perform holiday cheer for our families. And somewhere in the private moments — the drive home at 2 AM, the walk around the block in the cold, the shower where no one can see — we allow ourselves to feel the full weight of it. The fear. The doubt. The question: Did I make the right decision? But we put it away. We tuck it back inside. We return to the performance because that’s what leaders do. We carry the weight so others don’t have to. The Muscle Memory of Survival But here’s what I’ve learned across all those Decembers, across all those companies, across all those moments of doubt, fear, and calculation: We are stronger than we realize. More resilient than we give ourselves credit for. More capable than the anxiety suggests. I’ve seen companies that seemed dead in December roar back to life in February. I’ve watched entrepreneurs who thought they were finished find unexpected paths forward, discover investors who moved faster than expected, and land clients who believed in their vision despite the timing. I’ve been that entrepreneur. I’ve been weeks from shutting down, days from missing payroll, hours from admitting defeat — and somehow, through luck or will or the kindness of someone who believed, found a way through. The muscle memory of survival is real. Each December, we navigate; each crisis, we manage; each impossible decision we make builds the capacity to handle the next one. We become fluent in uncertainty. We develop an intimacy with fear that enables us to function in its presence instead of being paralyzed by it. We learn that we’re more capable of enduring what we once thought was unbearable than we ever imagined. The Collective Weight To every entrepreneur reading this while the world sleeps and you scroll through financial projections at midnight: You are not alone. To everyone who’s made the agonizing decision to let good people go in order to save the company: I’ve been there. Many times. The guilt doesn’t make you weak; it makes you human. The burden you bear is proof of your conscience, not your failure. To those waiting on term sheets that should have closed last month, watching the calendar with dread: Your frustration is valid. Your anxiety is real. And it’s not a reflection of your worth or your vision — it’s a reflection of the broken ecosystem that moves venture capital by committee and calendar rather than merit. To the founders who will spend the holidays pitching because you can’t afford not to: Your hustle is seen. Your dedication matters. The sacrifices you’re making while others celebrate are not going unnoticed by those who understand. To everyone carrying the weight of other people’s livelihoods on your shoulders: That responsibility is heavy, and you’re handling it with more grace than you probably give yourself credit for. The fact that it keeps you awake at night shows you’re the right person for the job. We Are With You I write this not from a place of having figured it all out, but from the trenches of experience. From the accumulated scar tissue of deals that fell apart, raises that took twice as long as projected, Decembers that tested every assumption I had about my resilience and capacity. From the memory of sitting in my car before going into a holiday party, trying to compose my face into something that wouldn’t worry my family. I write this because the venture capital world, the startup ecosystem, and the entire apparatus of entrepreneurship can feel isolating by design. We celebrate the wins publicly and suffer the struggles privately. We share the success stories on stages and in interviews, while remaining silent about the months we went without a salary, the nights we questioned everything, and the moments we thought about giving up. But there is strength in breaking that silence. Recognizing that the holiday season — with all its beauty and promise — is also a gauntlet that entrepreneurs must navigate while maintaining the illusion that everything is festive and fine. Acknowledging that December anxiety isn’t a sign of weakness; it’s wisdom. It’s the mark of someone who understands what’s at stake. The Light Beyond December The truth that I’ve learned, that I want to share is this: January arrives. Every time. The world gets back to work. Deals that were on hold during the holidays start moving again. Clients come back. Momentum begins to rebuild. The days get longer, and the light starts to return — both literally and figuratively. December feels eternal when you’re in it, but it’s not. It’s a tunnel, and there is light on the other side. Not guaranteed success — entrepreneurship offers no such promise — but opportunity. Another chance. Another shot at making it work. Another month to turn things around. And if this December feels especially tough, if the anxiety is more intense, if the decisions you’re facing seem impossible and the burden feels unbearable: know this — you’re not alone. We stand with you. Those of us who’ve walked this path, who’ve felt this weight in our chests at 3 AM, who’ve made the impossible calls, and lived to tell about it — we see you. We recognize the struggle. We understand the performance you’re maintaining. And we’re here — in solidarity, in understanding, in shared experience. The holiday lights will eventually come down. The world will return to its normal rhythm. The year will turn. And you — resilient, persistent, stubborn in the most beautiful way — you will still be standing. Still building. Still believing that what you’re creating matters, even when December tries to convince you otherwise. To All Who Carry This Weight This is a message from those in the trenches to those in the trenches. From someone who understands that entrepreneurship isn’t just about the victories, but about the vigils we keep when everyone else is resting. From someone who knows that the real work happens not on the stages where we’re invited to speak, but in the quiet moments when we’re alone with the numbers, the responsibility, and the knowledge that people are counting on us. We carry this together. The responsibility. The anxiety. The hope. The belief that what we’re building is worth the cost of these difficult Decembers. The knowledge that the struggle is real and the resilience required is extraordinary. From one entrepreneur to another, from someone who’s spent more Decembers in spreadsheets than in celebration, who knows that the path we’ve chosen is not the easy one: You’ve got this. Not because it’s easy, not because it’s certain, not because December will be kind to you — but because you’ve already proven you can survive what most people would consider impossible. That persistence, that resilience, that refusal to let December’s darkness define the story — that’s what makes you an entrepreneur.

slides.title: Burning Man: Beyond the Desert’s False Prophets
slides.subtitle: Vitaly Golomb on LinkedIn
slides.description: Photo credit: Jailbird Lilia ShirmanA week has passed since I returned from the playa, and I wanted my impressions to settle and marinade before sharing. The desert doesn’t lie. Unlike the critics who mock from their air-conditioned offices, the Black Rock Desert strips away pretense and reveals truth. This year, as I, along with my wife, co-led a 48-person camp through the crucible of 2025’s Burning Man, I witnessed something the haters will never understand: how shared adversity transforms strangers into family, how art becomes sacred space, and how the Japanese concept of Gaman — enduring hardship with dignity — creates bonds deeper than years of casual friendship. The Symphony of Storms and Souls The 2025 burn began not with music, but with the desert’s own percussion — winds that reached 52 miles per hour on Saturday night, tearing through Black Rock City like nature’s own reset button. These weren’t gentle breezes; they were 50-mph gusts that demolished camps, destroyed art installations, and yes, claimed the infamous Orgy Dome that critics love to fixate on. Surveying the damage to our camp mid-storm But here’s what the mockers miss: those storms weren’t obstacles — they were catalysts. When Ukrainian artist Oleksiy Sai’s massive “Black Cloud” installation was torn apart by hurricane-force winds on Ukrainian Independence Day, something remarkable happened. Communities that had been politely coexisting suddenly became families, strangers becoming brothers and sisters in the ancient ritual of shared struggle. Black Cloud being torn apart in the wind storm Lessons from Tokyo’s Furnace Coincidentally, we had visited Tokyo in July, struggling through Japan’s record-breaking summer — the hottest in 127 years of recorded history. The experience became an unexpected rehearsal for what awaited us on the playa, teaching us that the most meaningful experiences often emerge from the crucible of challenge rather than the ease of convenience. Tea ceremony in Tokyo - July 2025 The Resurrection of Ukrainian Art From the ashes of “Black Cloud” rose something even more powerful — “No Fate,” a testament to Ukrainian resilience. Oleksiy Sai and his team, led by producer Vitaliy Deynega of Ukrainian Witness, transformed the storm-destroyed installation into a new work within three days, using salvaged pieces of black Oxford fabric to spell out the phrase “No Fate” — shortened from Sarah Connor’s defiant cry in Terminator 2: “No fate but what we make”. Last year’s Burning Man was when I decided I needed to return to music after a decade and a half hiatus. This year brought a serendipitous opportunity to bring my joyous music to this solemn Ukrainian art installation — a resurrection of one art piece from another that perfectly demonstrated Ukrainian resilience. My performance was meant to show that life goes on, that we can thrive through anything, that even in the face of destruction, creativity endures and transforms. https://instagram.com/ViTALii.music The Temple of the Deep: Where Grief Becomes Gold At the heart of this year’s transformation stood Miguel Arraiz’s “Temple of the Deep” — a 44-foot-tall monument to the Japanese art of kintsugi, where broken pottery is repaired with gold to highlight rather than hide the cracks. The temple’s heptagonal design drew from the volcanic rocks of the Black Rock Desert itself, its seven entrances representing the seven stages of grief. This wasn’t decoration; it was architecture as philosophy. Like the Japanese concept of finding beauty in brokenness, the temple served as sacred space where 70,000 souls could process loss, transformation, and healing. When it burned on August 31st, it carried with it not just wood and flame, but the collective grief and hope of an entire temporary city. The Japanese Art of Desert Endurance The philosophy of Gaman — enduring unavoidable suffering with patience and dignity — found perfect expression on the playa this year. When Tuesday night’s thunderstorms created standing water that electrocuted one participant, requiring airlift to a trauma center, the desert was teaching its harshest lesson about resilience. Yet even as a man was airlifted into the night sky, even as gates closed and mud trapped vehicles, the deeper truth emerged: Shikata ga nai — what cannot be changed must be accepted, and from that acceptance comes strength. The Japanese understand that true growth happens not in comfort, but in the crucible of challenge. Our Village: Leadership in the Storm Leading our camp through months of planning had prepared us for logistics, but not for this level of testing. The drive itself became an ordeal — our Rivian’s battery draining faster than anticipated while towing supplies across Nevada, forcing us to pull a generator from the trailer just to charge while waiting in the entry line on Wednesday night of build week. Pushing the generator in the entry line along side the Rivian When those 52-mph winds hit Saturday night, destroying our bar structure along with installations across the city, our camp faced its first real test. But instead of fragmenting, we discovered something powerful: crisis reveals character. Camp members who’d barely known each other rallied together, rebuilding not just physical structures but forging emotional bonds that will outlast any temporary city. Jail of Hedone 2025 version 1.0 destroyed The Sacred Space of Authentic Connection Our bar, which we called “Jail of Hedone,” became something far more profound than its provocative name suggested. The playa creates conditions where complete strangers skip past small talk and dive straight into what truly matters — “sharing deeply, openly, without” the masks we wear in the default world. One campmate observed how visitors arrived with their own interpretations of our space, reactions as diverse as the playa itself. Within minutes, strangers would open up about intimate topics they’d never shared publicly, later expressing amazement at their own vulnerability. The magic lies in how the desert strips away pretense, creating a container where authentic human connection feels not just safe, but natural. Perhaps that’s the deeper meaning of our “Jail of Hedone” — true pleasure isn’t about excess or indulgence, but about the freedom to feel authentically. When the soul connects with genuine love and presence, pleasure becomes sacred rather than superficial, flowing from real connection rather than performance. Thursday’s Resurrection The rains that followed on Wednesday, forcing us to abandon our bikes at the temple and walk back through lightning and flooding, became pilgrimage rather than hardship. When Thursday’s sun finally broke through, drying the playa and allowing Black Rock City to truly come alive, the transformation felt biblical. After a week of exhausting challenges, everything suddenly crystallized — the unique privilege of watching our small community thrive as an island within the larger ecosystem of the playa became undeniable. This wasn’t relief; it was revelation. The hardships hadn’t been obstacles to overcome but ingredients in an alchemical process, transforming 48 individuals into a functioning village with its own culture, rituals, and unbreakable bonds. The Critics’ Comfortable Ignorance When I read the jokes about the collapsed Orgy Dome, the celebration that “all the terrible people are out of town,” the gleeful coverage of our weather challenges, I understand what I’m witnessing: the fear of transformation disguised as superiority. These critics reveal more about themselves than about Burning Man — they’re afraid to step outside comfort zones, afraid to face real challenges, afraid to discover who they might become when stripped of familiar defenses. The desert offers a mirror that reflects not just who you are, but who you could be. Those who mock it from safety are choosing cynicism over possibility, comfort over growth. Beyond the Music Festival Myth The greatest misconception persists: that Burning Man is primarily a music festival. While electronic beats pulse through desert nights, music is merely one thread in a vast tapestry of artistic expression. The 2025 theme “Tomorrow Today” brought together art installations from creators worldwide, transforming the temporary city into what may be the world’s most ambitious art laboratory. Long Feng Art Car This isn’t entertainment — it’s transformation. Your camp becomes art, your vehicle becomes art, your interactions with others become performance pieces in this grand experiment of human creativity. The Science of Sacred Bonds Research demonstrates that “pain is a particularly powerful ingredient in producing bonding and cooperation between those who share painful experiences”. Groups enduring challenging tasks together show significantly greater bonding than those completing easier activities, developing increased willingness to cooperate and sacrifice for the group’s benefit. This scientific finding explains why 40 hours of struggling through dust storms, equipment failures, and extreme conditions creates deeper connections than years of casual socializing. The shared ordeal becomes crucible, burning away superficial barriers and forging genuine bonds. JoH Team Rebuilding The Three-Day Transformation The unwritten “three-day rule” among veteran burners recognizes a profound truth: it takes approximately three days to fully disconnect from default world mentalities and embrace the playa’s transformative possibilities. This isn’t about adjusting to dust and heat — it’s about releasing the identity that career, possessions, and social status have created. This reset proves crucial for creativity to flourish. Breaking routine patterns and experiencing novel environments enhances creative thinking. On the playa, freed from normal social constraints and surrounded by constant artistic stimulus, participants discover aspects of themselves they never knew existed. Why the Desert Endures Burning Man succeeds not despite its hardships, but because of them. The dust storms, extreme weather, logistical challenges, and physical discomfort serve as crucible, transforming individual participants into genuine community. The Japanese understanding of growth through adversity — Gaman — plays out in real time as people discover reserves of strength, creativity, and compassion they never knew they possessed. The playa remains, patient and transformative, ready to teach anyone willing to learn its lessons about resilience, creativity, and the profound bonds that form when humans share both struggle and wonder beneath the vast desert sky. Those who mock from safety will never understand what they’re missing — not just a festival, but a laboratory for the human spirit, a temporary city where transformation becomes inevitable for those brave enough to enter its gates. In the end, whether witnessing Ukrainian art rise from storm-destroyed ashes or learning endurance in Tokyo’s summer heat, the desert doesn’t lie. It simply reveals who we are beneath our comfortable masks, and who we might become if we’re willing to endure the beautiful hardship of genuine growth.

slides.title: The Virtual Reality We Didn’t Expect: How Social Media Became Our Dystopian Digital Reality
slides.subtitle: Vitaly Golomb on LinkedIn
slides.description: When “Ready Player One” came out in 2018, like many in Silicon Valley, I viewed it as a prescient vision of our technological future. We were on the brink of what seemed like a VR revolution, with Oculus just around the corner and the promise of fully immersive digital worlds that would transform how we live, work, and connect. The tech industry collectively believed we were progressing toward a future where virtual reality would be as ubiquitous as smartphones, where digital avatars would replace physical presence, and where the boundaries between reality and simulation would blur in ways that enhanced human experience. Back then, the Valley was a place where every new startup was pitched as a force for positive change, and improving the world wasn’t just a tagline; it was a mission. But today, as someone who has spent decades building and supporting technology companies, I find myself increasingly shocked by what my industry is doing to the world. The virtual reality we got isn’t the one we expected — or the one we were promised. We were right about the blurred boundaries. We were catastrophically wrong about everything else. The Virtual Reality We Didn’t Expect: How Social Media Became Our Dominant Digital Reality The Great Technology Misdirection The data presents a sobering story about our technological trajectory. While the industry invested billions in VR development — companies like Meta alone contributing over $13 billion annually to their “metaverse” ambitions — the technology that truly captured and colonized human attention was far more insidious. Social media platforms, initially dismissed as mere communication tools, have become the dominant virtual reality of our time, creating immersive environments that prove far more addictive and psychologically manipulative than any headset-based experience we had ever imagined. The irony is profound: We worried about people losing themselves in fantasy worlds when, in reality, they were losing themselves in curated information bubbles designed to exploit their deepest psychological vulnerabilities. We built the infrastructure for a Ready Player One future, but instead of the OASIS, we got Facebook’s News Feed — a virtual space that weaponizes human psychology for profit while pretending to foster connection. I’m an interested amateur when it comes to politics, but I can’t help but notice how the very platforms we celebrated for “connecting the world” have ended up weaponizing the worst of human nature. The Valley’s shift from idealistic liberalism to a form of rapid libertarianism — where “move fast and break things” is an ethos, not a warning — has left us with a digital landscape optimized for profit, not progress. The Weaponization of Human Nature What social media platforms discovered, and what we in the venture capital world initially celebrated as “engagement optimization,” was actually the systematic exploitation of evolutionary psychology. The human brain, evolved for small tribal groups, was never designed to process the constant stream of social comparison, outrage, and dopamine manipulation that defines modern social media. The platforms have learned to weaponize what researchers call the “comparison trap” — the innate tendency to measure our worth against others. However, unlike traditional social comparison within actual communities, social media has created an infinite scroll of curated highlights, filtered perfection, and manufactured controversy designed to keep users engaged at any psychological cost. As a result, a generation is experiencing unprecedented levels of anxiety, depression, and social isolation, despite being more “connected” than ever before. The Mental Health Catastrophe The data on the mental health impact of social media is unequivocal and devastating. Between 2005 and 2017, depression among young people rose by 52%, with the steepest increase directly correlating to the widespread adoption of social platforms. Each additional hour of social media usage raises the depression risk by 13% in adolescents, with young women experiencing a 172% increase in depression risk compared to pre-social media baselines. The Mental Health Crisis: Youth Depression Rises with Social Media Growth Social Media’s Unequal Mental Health Burden: Young People Hit Hardest What’s especially alarming is how this mental health crisis intersects with a broader societal breakdown. Young men, already facing declining economic prospects and shifting social expectations, have increasingly found themselves isolated in digital spaces that provide the illusion of connection without its substance. Dating apps have transformed courtship into a consumerist marketplace, while social media has created unrealistic standards and expectations that make authentic relationship formation increasingly difficult. The Assault on Family Formation The impact on family formation has been profound and multifaceted. Social media has fundamentally changed how young people develop relationship skills, creating what sociologists call a “dating apocalypse,” where the abundance of choice paradoxically leads to commitment avoidance. The platforms’ addiction to engagement metrics means they profit from keeping users single, scrolling, and emotionally available for advertising rather than fostering stable family units. The economic data is equally concerning. Areas with higher social media engagement reveal stronger correlations with economic inequality, as platforms generate digital divides that reflect and amplify existing socioeconomic disparities. Young people in lower-income areas are more inclined to consume passive entertainment content, while those in wealthier areas engage with news and educational material, creating a feedback loop that reinforces class stratification. The New Southern Strategy: Digital Division Perhaps most dangerously, political actors quickly recognized social media’s potential as a tool for manipulation and division. What we’re witnessing is essentially the Southern Strategy on steroids — the systematic exploitation of social and racial anxieties, now amplified by algorithmic systems designed to maximize engagement through emotional provocation. Social media’s impact on democracy–both nourishing and undermining. The original Southern Strategy operated by employing coded language and cultural symbols to trigger racial resentment while retaining plausible deniability. Social media platforms have intensified this method by creating echo chambers where partisan content is algorithmically amplified, ensuring that users primarily encounter information that supports their existing beliefs, while growing increasingly hostile toward opposing viewpoints. The result is a political environment where 89% of Trump supporters and 90% of Biden supporters believed that the opposing party’s victory would cause lasting harm to America. For the record, unfortunately, the Democrats weren’t wrong. But this isn’t natural polarization — it’s the inevitable outcome of systems designed to keep users engaged through manufactured outrage and reinforcement of tribal identity. Political polarization in the media age. The Corporate Capture of Democracy The intersection of social media manipulation with campaign finance deregulation has created a perfect storm for democratic dysfunction. The Citizens United decision in 2010 opened the floodgates for unlimited corporate spending in elections, coinciding almost exactly with the rise of social media platforms as primary news sources. The outcome has been the emergence of what I call “algorithmic gerrymandering” — the ability to micro-target political messages and disinformation to specific demographics with surgical precision. In the 2024 election alone, super PACs spent over $4.5 billion, with much of that money flowing through social media advertising systems designed to amplify divisive content. Elon Musk’s $280 million investment in Republican candidates illustrates how easily billionaires can now leverage both platform ownership and campaign finance loopholes to shape democratic outcomes. The Legislative Imperative The current regulatory framework is not just inadequate; it actively enables the problems we face. Section 230, written in 1996 when the internet was a fundamentally different ecosystem, grants social media companies broad immunity from liability for user-generated content while imposing no corresponding obligations on how their algorithms amplify and monetize that content. Recent bipartisan efforts to sunset Section 230 represent a crucial first step. However, as someone who has paid attention to how quickly legislators can be influenced by industry lobbying, I believe we need more than piecemeal reform. We require comprehensive legislation that addresses three critical areas: Algorithmic Accountability Platforms should lose Section 230 protections for algorithmically amplified content. If a company’s algorithm decides to promote specific content to maximize engagement, it should bear responsibility for the consequences. This would preserve free speech protections for genuine user expression while holding companies accountable for their editorial choices disguised as neutral algorithms. Campaign Finance Reform Citizens United must be overturned through constitutional amendment if necessary. The combination of unlimited corporate spending and micro-targeted social media advertising has created an environment where democratic outcomes can be purchased by the highest bidder. We cannot have a functioning democracy when billionaires can spend hundreds of millions to influence elections through opaque super PAC structures. Child Protection Measures Recent bipartisan legislation such as the Kids Off Social Media Act exemplifies the kind of evidence-based intervention we need. Establishing minimum age requirements, eliminating algorithmic targeting of minors, and mandating parental consent for teen accounts are common-sense measures that prioritize child development over corporate profits. Beyond the Current Crisis The virtual reality we’ve created through social media represents one of the greatest market failures in technological history. We built systems optimized for engagement and advertising revenue instead of human flourishing, and the results speak for themselves: rising mental illness, political dysfunction, economic inequality, and social isolation on an unprecedented scale in human history. I didn’t get into technology to build systems that make people miserable or undermine democracy. Most of my peers didn’t either. But somewhere along the way, the Valley’s dream of making the world better got hijacked by a relentless focus on growth, engagement, and libertarian dogma. As investors and entrepreneurs, we bear a responsibility to recognize that our industry’s relentless focus on growth and engagement metrics has produced negative externalities that jeopardize the foundation of democratic society. The platforms we have funded and celebrated have, in many ways, become the dystopian virtual reality we feared — not because they transport us to fictional worlds, but because they have replaced genuine human connection with algorithmic manipulation designed to extract maximum value from our attention and emotional responses. The path forward requires both regulatory intervention and a fundamental shift in how we think about technology’s role in society. We need platforms designed for human flourishing instead of profit maximization, democratic accountability rather than algorithmic opacity, and genuine connection rather than manufactured engagement. The virtual reality we create going forward will determine whether technology serves humanity or humanity serves technology. The virtual reality we’re living in wasn’t what we intended to create. However, it’s not too late to change direction — if we have the courage to acknowledge where we went wrong and the determination to do better. The choice is ours, but time is running out. Every day we postpone meaningful reform, another generation grows up in a digital environment designed to exploit rather than empower them. The metaverse Mark Zuckerberg promises may never come to fruition, but the dystopian social media reality we’re facing is already here — and it’s time we take responsibility for creating something better. And it’s frightening to think of how AI will further accelerate our rapid descent toward this place we don’t want to be.

slides.title: The Dual Predators of Startup Ecosystems: Fake Bankers and Exploitative Conferences
slides.subtitle: Vitaly Golomb on LinkedIn
slides.description: After over two decades in Silicon Valley as an entrepreneur, venture capitalist, and investment banker, I’ve seen the best and worst of the startup world. I’ve put on startup education events in a dozen countries, working to empower founders with fundamental knowledge and connections. That’s why, as an investor and investment banker, nothing pisses me off more than the bottom-feeder fake “investment bankers” and predatory conference organizers who exploit founders’ hopes and fears. The Florida Connection: A Breeding Ground for Financial Predators If your startup has gained even modest visibility, you’ve probably received emails from self-proclaimed matchmakers claiming they “represent a specific family office investor interested in your sector and that you would be an excellent fit for their portfolio.” These operators often cluster in Florida, taking advantage of the state’s favorable regulatory environment and growing tech reputation to conceal their inexperience. Their tactics follow a predictable formula: Unsolicited outreach with subject lines like “{Name} quick question.” Immediate retainer demands bait and switch to represent your startup to their network with an immediate retainer before any actionable work begins. Fictitious track records — many “partners” lack even junior-level experience at reputable firms. One “banker” I encountered, operating from Boca Raton, had graduated college just four years prior and previously sold timeshares. Yet his firm claimed to specialize in Series B raises for SaaS companies — a clear red flag. The Conference Trap: $2,500 Tables and Mirage Investor Access Parallel to the fake banker epidemic, major startup conferences have become sophisticated extraction machines. Events now routinely charge founders $2,500–$5,000 for basic exhibition tables, plus hidden fees ($1,050 for Wi-Fi, $232 for electricity), while promising “curated investor meetings.” The reality? These fees often exceed early-stage marketing budgets yet deliver less value than a targeted LinkedIn campaign. Bait-and-Switch Tactics: One major event recently offered an “Investor Pass” for several hundred dollars, granting access to unnamed “top VCs,” while funneling attendees to junior analysts compiling market maps — not decision-makers. Volume Over Quality: At another well-known conference, dozens of seed-stage founders paid up to $2,000 to pitch mid-level associates from second-tier funds lacking check-writing authority. Predatory Economics: Analysis of tens of thousands of conference interactions found that over 90% of “investor meetings” led nowhere, yet organizers still tout “social media impressions” as ROI. The CEO’s Two Mandates: Hiring and Runway Preservation As a founder, your priorities are non-negotiable: Hire Exceptional Talent: Your early team dictates trajectory more than any pitch deck. Conserve Cash: Every dollar spent on fake bankers or conferences shortens your runway. Predators exploit the second mandate by monetizing desperation. A $25k retainer to a fake banker or $10k conference package could instead fund several months of a critical engineer’s salary — an investment with measurable ROI. When Professional Services Actually Add Value Legitimate investment banking and strategic conferences have their place — but only at specific stages: Investment Banking Threshold: $20M+ Raises Economic Viability: Bankers typically charge 3–7% success fees. On a $20M raise, this aligns incentives (bankers earn $600k–$1.4M) while being feasible for the company. Investor Complexity: Later-stage rounds involve multi-layered term sheets, international funds, and regulatory hurdles where experienced advisors prove invaluable. Conference Participation: Post-Product-Market Fit Strategic Networking: Use events after securing initial funding to forge partnerships, not investor pitches. Selective Attendance: Target niche gatherings for exposure or enterprise sales, rather than generic “startup” events. Fortifying Your Startup Against Exploitation with Due Diligence Banker Vetting: Ask for past deal lists and speak to founders you identify, not provided references. Many jurisdictions, especially in the U.S., require licenses to work in the securities industry; verify them. Conference ROI Analysis: Use tools to track lead conversion rates — most booth leads never progress beyond the initial contact. Calculate cost per SQL (sales-qualified lead). If exceeding $500, decline. Financial Safeguards The IB Model: Legitimate bankers will require retainers but tie 90%+ of their fees to successful raises. For this reason, they will be selective in what projects they sign on to. Fake bankers are retainer mills collecting $10k-25k checks from dozens or hundreds of first-time founders and will sign up anyone. Outcome-Based Conference Fees: Negotiate partial refunds if promised investor meetings don’t materialize. Conclusion: Prioritizing Substance Over Illusion The path to startup success is littered with predators — from Florida-based “bankers” to conference organizers selling overpriced hope. Your antidote is ruthless prioritization: Delay external fundraising help until you’re seeking $20M+. Early rounds depend on founder-investor relationships, not intermediaries. Reinvest conference budgets into product development and hiring. The best investors find you through traction, not exhibition halls. Treat advisors like hires — require verified track records, transparent pricing, and skin in the game. I’ve dedicated my career to helping founders avoid these traps because real opportunities don’t come through cold emails or booth receipts. They’re built through relentless execution, strategic hires, and capital efficiency — the very priorities these predators encourage you to neglect. Don’t let them.

publications.title: Time-reversal of Waves for Spatial Focusing of Signals in Enclosures: Targeted Wireless Communications
publications.description: Time-reversal is the process whereby a signal is emitted by a source and propagates in a medium with scatterers in it. The waves are recorded at a receiver over a time much larger than the original pulse duration so as to capture the multiple scattering. The receiver then reverses the waveform in time and re-emits it into the same channel. The waves back-propagate through the medium retracing the multiple scattering paths and ultimately refocus at the original source location in space and time. Time-reversal in an enclosure with a single detector achieves spatial focusing of the energy to within one half of a wavelength of the initial sound signal. A two- dimensional finite-difference time-domain code was calibrated to study the phenomena of time compression and spatial focusing of time-reversed acoustic signals in closed environments with strong reverberations. One of our main results is that time-reversal in enclosures with a keyhole aperture of size comparable to the width of the initial wave front achieves tight spatial focusing of the acoustic field at the source. We show that time-reversal can deliver trains of pulses to desired locations.

publications.title: Optimization of scattering resonances
publications.description: The increasing use of micro- and nano-scale components in optical, electrical, and mechanical systems makes the understanding of loss mechanisms and their quantification issues of fundamental importance. In this paper we study the problem of systematically improving a structure by altering its design so as to decrease the loss of radiating waves into the surrounding area. We use sensitivity analysis and local gradient optimiztaion, applie dto the scatteringresonance problem, to reduce the loss within the class of piecewise constant structures.

about:
As the Global Talent Attraction Assistant Director at EY, with a specialized focus on tax recruitment since December 2015, I have played a pivotal role in steering the tax talent acquisition strategies within the firm's Regional, National, and Financial Services Tax Practices. My tenure of over eight years in the Greater Los Angeles area has been characterized by a resolute dedication to tailoring recruitment practices to meet the unique demands of the tax sector, ensuring alignment with EY's strategic objectives for growth. I have been committed to refining the tax recruitment processes and fostering an environment of inclusion and belonging, an effort that is exemplified by my attainment of the EY Better Us - Inclusion and Belonging - Bronze Learning certification in 2024.

Prior to my current role, I served as a Recruiting Manager for Financial Due Diligence at PwC from September 2013 to September 2015. There, I honed my ability to craft and implement search strategies that successfully sourced financial consultants pivotal to the firm's success. I was a Sourcing Manager Walgreens from December 2011 to September 2013 ensured the recruitment of individuals who not only possessed the necessary skills but also resonated with the company's vibrant retail culture.

My experience as Talent Acquisition Consultant at Sapient for a year in the Greater Chicago Area allowed me to streamline hiring processes and significantly improve the caliber of new hires for essential roles. Similarly, my year-long consultancy at talentRISE solidified my reputation for delivering strategic recruitment solutions that bolstered the firm's standing as a leader in talent services. Each of these roles has contributed to my extensive expertise in talent acquisition and management, shaping me into a leader adept at navigating the complexities of the recruitment landscape.

headline: Retired EY Partner
about:
After 37 years, I retired from EY on June 30, 2019. EY has been a significant part of my life, and as I reflect back on my time at EY it’s truly been an incredible experience. When I started in the Chicago office, I never could have imagined all of the great experiences I would have along the way working in the Chicago, Century City, Tokyo and San Jose offices, and traveling to so many other cities and countries during my journey. Most importantly, it’s about working with great people and all the friendships, relationships and experiences we have shared. I want to thank you all for being a part of my great experience at EY. I look forward to keeping in touch.

As a Partner in EY’s San Jose office, I had over 20 years of transaction advisory experience serving technology clients and 37 years of business experience. I had the opportunity to serve a number of leading and high-growth technology companies with acquisitions, investments, carve-outs and divestitures. I led many cross-border and global technology deals involving numerous countries.

From 2014 to 2017, I was the Americas Inbound/Outbound Transaction Advisory Services Leader. In this role, I focused on working with global EY account teams and our multinational clients outside of the US that were looking to invest, acquire or divest businesses in the Americas. 

From 2006 to 2014, I was EY’s Global Technology Transaction Advisory Leader. During this time I focused on enabling our transactions teams to deliver exceptional client service to help our clients achieve their strategic objectives around acquisitions and divestitures. My observations about technology M&A trends have been featured in Bloomberg, The Wall Street Journal, the Financial Times, The Economist, Forbes, Barron’s, Reuters, Dow Jones and VentureBeat.

He organized 4 Asian Leadership conferences and first time won 3 global awards and is experiencing exponential growth of about 122% in membership (vs. 31% globally) and 311% growth in number of PMP's (vs. 67% globally).
 
He has demonstrated his interest in Project Management profession when he became a qualified PMP.  Since then he has contributed in several ways to PM profession by publishing books and papers on Project Management.

Ay Yi Yai Yi!  We are in the middle of The New World Order!

Empires rise, decline, and fall. History has witnessed this cycle with the Romans, the Ottomans, and the British. They have all toppled, and if we are not careful, the US will be the next.

Many of today’s enterprises are a gaggle of debt-addicted extreme financial engineering frogs floundering in tepid snake oil. Unfortunately, many will find their demise in the clutches of IP vultures.

publications.title: My OD Dissertation Journey: Ph.D. Student, to Ph.D. Candidate, to Ph.D., to Terminal Degree Holder
publications.description: I share my OD dissertation journey from the first-person perspective because it reflects my thoughts and experience in a cohort-style learning environment with world-class OD guest lecturers, which exposed me to top OD associations and scholar-practitioners who have contributed to cutting-edge OD research.

publications.title: “Exploring the Role of the OD Consultant: Historical Perspectives and Contemporary Findings.”
publications.description: The purpose of this study was to explore the lived experience of contemporary OD consultants to better understand their knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as their work experiences, perceptions and challenges. This paper includes the unexpected finding of the alignment of contemporary OD consultants’ words to the OD classical writings of roughly 40 years earlier. These 2020 OD consultants' words and values aligned with the classical OD works and views of scholars from decades ago.

publications.title: The Evolving World of the OD Consultant: Sharing the ‘Now’ and Future with Current Findings
publications.description: In alignment with the theme of this year’s ODN conference, we will present the work and impact of today’s OD consultants as described by 40 consultants in 2020. Textbooks for Organization Development often begin with the history and the background of OD. However, newcomers to OD are interested in the OD consultant, what the work of an OD consultant ‘looks like,’ and which industry OD consultants work in. Now is the time to explore the who and where of today’s OD consultants, and where OD is making an impact!

publications.title: Organization Development Consultation: Collaborative Partnerships
publications.description: Consultation is an inquiring and helping relationship; it is an aligned trusted relationship (D. Jamieson, personal communication, September 13, 2019). "Organization Development consultants offer consultation on the process used to reach a desired goal" (Anderson, 2020, p. 11). "Values distinguish organization development (OD) from other methods of consulting and change. One of these differences relates to the values of OD work. Focusing interventions and the consulting process to ensure growth, development, and learning is a key-value" (Anderson, 2020, p. 50). The presentation explored the phenomenon of organization development consultation. The knowledge generated from this inquiry affords new insights into organization development and also informs consultation.

publications.title: The Who, The How, The What of OD Consulting
publications.publishedAt: Academy of Management (AoM)-ODC & MC Divisions, ISODC, and ISEOR Conference Lyon, France · Jun 16, 2020
publications.description: Practicing the who, the how, and the what of planned change differs across situations in various organizations. According to Cummings and Worley (2015), organization development is based on improving organizational effectiveness. Organization development involves the consulting process of pre-entering, entering, contracting, diagnosing, intervening, evaluating, and terminating of change by external consultants and internal consultants. I share my research journey from the first-person perspective because it reflects my thoughts. I hope to unify the significance and vision from my experience in the organization development field with the diverse theoretical dialogues; to assist in influencing consultation literature's importance and relevance to organization development scholar- practitioners (Golden-Biddle & Locke, 2007).

publications.title: Developing the Whole Organization Development Consultant in Order to Change the Organizational World
publications.description: The study of the education and professional development of Organization Development Consultants: My Scholar-Practitioner Journey.

publications.title: The Practice of Planned Change: The Who, How, What?
publications.description: Critics have suggested several problems with the way planned change is carried out. Their concern is not with the planned change model itself, but with how change takes place and with the skills, knowledge, emotional intelligence, experience, and interventions used by consultants. This presentation looks at how teams of internal and external consultants work together to practice transformational change.

publications.title: “Human Innovators” – Reinventing Community Colleges at CCC: Seven Colleges-One Incubator Illinois Council Community College Administrators (ICCCA), 2014.
publications.description:
Higher education is slow to change, especially when it comes to college or system-wide shifts like strategic plans, software implementations, or process improvement. CCC has opted for a unique business model that embeds seven strategists into each college, also known as Directors of Strategic Initiatives, to be human “agents of change.” The goal is to complete projects swiftly while balancing institutional consensus, all while sharing the workload with college faculty, administrators, staff and students. The position is not for the faint of heart and was originally created as a project manager for each President and to support District-wide initiatives. The role has evolved into a tight-knit team that works collectively with District and the college and serves as an incubator for innovation and performance dialogs with strong institutional influence. The role has become a key component for executing major projects (from budgets to student success tools) and supporting performance improvement.
	The presentation will focus on the following: Overview of CCC & Reinvention Initiative; the Hybrid Academic / Business Consultant  Operational Model & Reinvention7; the DSI Role: Strategic planning, data driven decision support, and strategic execution; the DSI System-Team Approach; and applying this model to your campus.

about:
Victor Lopez serves as a Senior Consultant in the FSO AI & Data practice within Technology Consulting at EY, based in New York City, NY. 

Victor earned a Master of Science in Information Systems and Analytics and a Bachelor of Science in Information Technology from Loyola University Chicago. During his university studies, he consistently achieved Dean’s Highest Honors and was recognized with the Turing High Achievement Award.

With three years of work experience in the metal and mining sector, Victor has held roles as a Senior HRIS Analyst, IT Technician, and IT Intern. 

His coursework and professional experiences have equipped him with in-depth knowledge of system configuration and data analytics. He has also honed a keen attention to detail, along with strong analytical and quantitative skills.

headline: Senior Partner (Retired) at EY
about:
Jim retired from Ernst & Young (EY) effective June 30th, 2019. Throughout his forty-year career, Jim served many of the firm’s largest global clients and fulfilled senior leadership roles within the firm. He developed deep insights into relationships and governance practices among boards, senior management and their auditors; gaining extensive knowledge of SEC financial reporting rules and regulations; familiarity with corporate financial staff organization and development; and experience with reporting and integration of mergers and acquisitions. Jim’s responsibilities were focused in the manufacturing, consumer products, technology and automotive sectors. Jim also held significant recruiting, people development and training responsibilities.

Jim holds an MBA in Accounting, Finance and International Business from The University of Chicago Booth Graduate School of Business and a Bachelor of Science in Accountancy from DePaul University and is both a Certified Public Accountant (CPA) and a Certified Management Accountant (CMA). Jim has also taught many EY training programs as well graduate accounting classes at DePaul University. He has served for several years on the DePaul University, Richard H. Driehaus College of Business advisory council and currently on the Board of Trustees of the University as Vice-Chair of the audit committee and member of the finance committee, as of 2017.

Jim has and continues to serve several non-for-profit organizations, including, The Archbishop Iakovos Leadership 100 Endowment Fund where he serves as Chairman of the Board of Trustees, The Board of National Hellenic Museum; as Founder and Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the Hellenic American Academy, one of the largest Greek-American schools in the United States as well as founding Chairman of the Foundation for Hellenic Education and Culture.

Jim serves on the Board of Directors of the Republic Bank of Chicago, the Board of Directors of Viveon Health Acquisition Corp. and as a member of the Advisory Council of CrossCountry Consulting.

Jim is originally from Greece having immigrated to the United States with his parents at the age of thirteen. He is married to Marianna and together they have three married children and nine grandchildren. His interests include spending time with his family, studying political science and world history, and playing golf.  He speaks the Modern Greek language fluently and has a basic understanding of German.

profileTopEducation.schoolName: University of Chicago Booth School of Business Executive Education

experience.description:
Jim served as Lead Partner for some of EY’s largest and most prestigious clients, including several Fortune 250 companies (The Coca-Cola Company, Fiat Chrysler Automobiles, Fiat Industrial, Whirlpool Corporation, Newell-Rubbermaid, Brunswick Corporation, Grainger and Molex Electronics) and several large private companies including Johnson Diversey. His boardroom experience includes more than 500 audit committee and board meetings. 

Jim held several EY leadership roles, from offices in Chicago, Frankfurt (Germany), New York, London and Atlanta. He served as Vice-Chair of Global Accounts (currently the G360 program), Managing Partner of the Midwest U.S assurance and advisory practices, Chairman of the German Business Center in the United States and as Managing Partner of the Consumer Products practice in Chicago.

Jim was elected by his partners to the Americas Partner Advisory Council where he served as Chairman during the sale of the then EY consulting practice to Cap Gemini, the firm Chairman succession process in 2000 and the merger discussions with another of the big four firms that ultimately was not completed. He was also elected to the first Global Advisory Council which formed and initiated the EY global organization strategy and many important related initiatives.

While serving six-years in Frankfurt, Germany, he was responsible for the coordination of all EY services, including audit and financial due diligence across Europe to several U.S. public companies and served as an adviser on SEC and U.S. GAAP matters to the German practice.

Jim also served as chair and/or member of senior EY committees responsible for the development and implementation of numerous global and America-wide strategy, operations and client service initiatives. From a Go-To-Market prospective, Jim participated on many related initiatives and proposals across the globe and personally led EY teams to winning five Fortune 500 Company audit proposals during his tenure as a Partner.

publications.title: Business Resilience: Weathering the Next Storm
publications.description:
In the first quarter of 2018, EY in association with the University of Calgary’s Haskayne School of Business conducted a survey of 70 executives from organizations in Canada’s oil and gas industry to gain insight into how those organizations achieved resilience during the past three years of continued low commodity prices.

This report summarizes the findings and provides insights into how companies achieved resilience and how they aim to position themselves in the next upturn. While the findings are specific to oil and gas companies, the components of resilience explored in this report are applicable to companies in other resource and energy based sectors.

publications.title: Canadian oil and gas reorganizations: From surviving to thriving in challenging times
publications.description:
In December 2016, EY, in association with the University of Calgary’s Haskayne School of Business — Executive Education, conducted a survey of more than 70 organizations in Canada’s oil and gas industry to gain insight into how they responded to continued low commodity prices. 

Our report summarizes the survey findings and identifies trends and common success factors by breaking responses down by not only company size and industry sector, but also by self-assessed levels of reorganization success.

publications.title: Accelerate your 3D technology journey in oil and gas
publications.description: Thirty-six percent of companies are already applying or intend to apply 3DP, according to a recent EY global survey of 900 companies. But, adoption in the energy and resources sector has been slow. In this piece of thought leadership, we look at the current state of 3D printing in the oil & gas industry as well as some of the areas of future potential for the technology.

publications.title: The trends, sector use cases and steps to accelerate your 3D printing journey
publications.description: Additive manufacturing, better known in the market as 3D printing (3DP), has been evolving over the past 30 years. There is growing evidence that the advancements in technology and materials have finally brought it beyond the hype stage. Our report looks at these advancements and the potential the technology has to change numerous industries in the coming years.

publications.title: Innovation: from ideation to activation
publications.description: In summer 2015, EY, in partnership with the UofC Hunter Centre for Entrepreneurship and Innovation, conducted a survey of more than 250 Canadian organizations across sector and industry. Executive leaders from a representative sample of large and small organizations from across Canada participated. In this report, we break down the results, and provide additional insight, using six key building blocks necessary for any innovation strategy.

publications.title: Roughin' It: The Anatomy of the Game
publications.description: Being one of Canada's national sports (a title it has shared since hockey was crowned a national sport in 1994), Lacrosse is still a relatively foreign sport to many Canadians. With the rise of the National Lacrosse League, I took a look at the game itself and why this sport may finally be appealing to Canadians.

projects.title: Bachelor Thesis
projects.description:
Abstratct:

The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has long been shaped by conflict, resource mismanagement, and extractive governance structures rooted in colonial history. Following independence, political elites and military leaders perpetuated exploitative practices, leaving the country vulnerable during periods of intense conflict. At the same time, China expanded its global resource strategy, employing approaches of flexigemony and resource diplomacy—adapting to the unique political and economic environments of African states to secure critical resources.

In the case of the DRC, these strategies have been criticized as “neo-colonial.” However, my thesis argues that China has largely adapted to the pre-existing extractive environment rather than creating it, leveraging agreements such as Sicomines within its broader diplomatic framework. This dynamic has nonetheless deepened structural challenges for the DRC. To counter this, the research highlights the role of Congolese agency—including state institutions, elites, and emerging actors like the Battery Council—as a critical lens for rethinking resource governance and balancing external influence.

headline: Energy Transition Leader | Board Advisor | EY Global Coordinating Partner | EY Americas Energy & Resources Power & Utilities
about:
The energy sector is transforming significantly, shaped by decarbonization, renewable
integration, and digitalization. I advise clients on navigating these complexities with a focus on
advancing the energy transition, modernizing grid and water infrastructure, and embedding
digital technologies. My work centers on building resilient, future-ready organizations that deliver
sustainable growth and long-term value in an evolving market.

As an EY Global Coordinating Partner, and former Americas Energy & Resources Industry Leader, I advise boards and executive teams on operational improvements, digital transformation strategies, and
navigating the risks and trade-offs associated with emerging technologies, including AI,
e-mobility, and smart grid innovation. I have more than 30 years of leadership experience across
Power and Utilities, Water and Wastewater, Oil and Gas, and Chemicals.

Previously, I also served as EY’s Americas Power and Utilities Sector Leader and Lead Client
Partner for three of the firm's largest energy clients, guiding enterprise-wide innovation and
transformation initiatives to support their journeys toward net-zero emissions. Over the course of
my career, I have led global teams across the United States, Latin America, Canada, India, and
the Philippines, delivering successful strategic outcomes in both mature and emerging markets.

In addition to my client work, I am committed to advancing diversity and inclusion across the
energy sector. I actively support the development of women executives through EY’s Women in
Energy Network and the Women’s Energy Network, and I lead the Power Energy Network, an
initiative focused on growing minority-owned businesses serving the energy industry.

I believe that strong leadership, diverse perspectives, and continuous innovation are essential to
building a clean energy future, and I am dedicated to helping shape that future across both
energy and water ecosystems.

honorsAndAwards.title: INROADS Rising Star Award
honorsAndAwards.description:
In 1970, Frank C. Carr, INROADS’ late founder, planted the seeds for what INROADS has become today. Inspired by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s landmark “I Have a Dream” speech, Frank quit his executive-level corporate day job in Chicago, IL and made a commitment to taking swift and decisive action to increase ethnically diverse employees in corporate management in the US, and to help change the way these candidates gained entry into the business world.
 The INROADS mission is to develop and place talented underserved youth in business and in industry, and prepare them for corporate and community leadership. From its founding in 1970 by business executive Frank C. Carr, ( MLK 1995 Salute to Greatness Recipient) INROADS has grown into a nationally recognized 501 © (3) nonprofit, impacting the lives of over 154,000 underrepresented youth, with over 50% being girls of color. 
The Rising Star Award recognizes individuals who has demonstrated exceptional leadership as well as embody and honor the INROADS mission. I was awarded based off my involved in the community with Junior Achievement, my continued support through leadership at EY and contribution with INROADS through mentoring students at Kennesaw State University all while serving as INROADS Alumni Association Vice President. My involvement in Securing funds and conducting the INROADS Alumni Association and EY Leadership Panel (The Art of Inclusion: Building a Diverse Team for a Diverse World) in March 2018, aligns with the mission of INROADS.
 The Benefit Gala’s goal serves as INROADS’ signature, most high-profile event. This charitable affair recognizes the achievements of our students, community/philanthropic leadership and honors corporate responsibility. As an honoree, I joined previous recipients, some of which have included ¬¬¬-Will & Jada Smith Family Foundation, XEOX’s former CEO Ursula Burns, PWC’s CEO Tim Ryan and General & Mrs. Colin Powell.
